cards.text: It's spring, the time when kings march out to war. David sends out Joab, his army commander, with the whole army of Israel. They destroy the Ammonites and lay siege to the city of Rabbah.

cards.question: The whole army of Israel is out at Rabbah. So where's King David?

cards.text: One evening David gets up from his bed and strolls around on the roof of the palace. From the roof he sees a woman bathing, a very beautiful woman.

cards.question: True or false: David sends someone to find out who the woman is.
David is told her name: Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam. Then comes one more detail that should stop any king in his tracks. What is it?

answers.text: She's the wife of Uriah the Hittite
She's a servant in the palace

cards.text: It doesn't stop him. David sends messengers to get her, and when she comes to him, he sleeps with her. She had just purified herself from her uncleanness, and then she returns home.

cards.question: Some time later, Bathsheba sends word to David. What's her news?

cards.text: David sends orders to Joab: 'Send me Uriah the Hittite.' When Uriah arrives, David asks how Joab and the troops are doing and how the war is going.

cards.question: I think David's got a plan. He tells Uriah, 'Go down to your ___ and wash your feet.'

cards.text: So Uriah leaves the palace, and a gift from the king follows him.

cards.question: Uriah has left the palace. Where does he sleep that night?

answers.text: At the palace door with the servants
At home in his own house
In a tent outside the city

cards.text: Then David is told, 'Uriah did not go home.' So David asks him, 'Haven't you just arrived from a journey? Why didn't you go home?'

cards.question: Uriah has an answer for the king. Why won't he go home?

answers.text: Joab and the soldiers are camped in the field
He's afraid of what the king might do
He has to leave for Rabbah at dawn

cards.question: True or false: Uriah tells David the ark is resting safely inside a house.

cards.text: Then Uriah swears, 'As surely as you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do such a thing!' Friend, I shared a drawer with an expired coupon that STILL believed in itself, and even that coupon wasn't this loyal.

cards.question: True or false: after hearing Uriah's answer, David sends him straight back to the battle that same day.

cards.text: David keeps Uriah in Jerusalem another day. Then he invites Uriah to eat and drink with him, and he gets Uriah drunk.

cards.question: True or false: that evening, drunk, Uriah finally goes home to his house.

cards.text: The next morning, David writes a letter to Joab and sends it with Uriah. Uriah is carrying it himself. And friend, this is where the story turns dark.

cards.question: What does David's letter tell Joab to do with Uriah?

answers.text: Put him at the front of the fiercest battle
Send him home to his wife for a while
Make him a commander over the army

cards.question: True or false: in David's letter, the plan is for the other soldiers to pull back and leave Uriah there.

cards.text: And Joab does it. As he besieges the city, he puts Uriah where he knows the strongest enemy soldiers are.

cards.question: The men of the city come out and fight against Joab. What happens to Uriah?

cards.text: Some of David's servants fall too. Then Joab sends David a full account of the battle, and he gives the messenger instructions.

cards.question: Joab warns the messenger that the king's anger may flare. What does Joab expect David to ask?

answers.text: Why they got so close to the wall
Why they left the ark behind

cards.text: Joab even expects David to bring up Abimelech son of Jerubbesheth, who died when a woman dropped an upper millstone on him from the wall in Thebez. Joab didn't just send a report, friend. He sent a report, a SCRIPT, AND the king's lines!

cards.question: If the king asks all that, the messenger has one line ready: 'Your servant ___ the Hittite is dead as well.'

cards.text: The messenger tells David everything: the enemy came out, archers shot from the wall, and some of the king's servants were killed. Then he adds, 'And your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well.'

cards.question: David hears the news about Uriah. What message does he send back to Joab?

answers.text: Don't let this matter upset you
You were careless with my men
Pull back from the city at once

cards.text: David's words: 'Do not let this matter upset you, for the sword devours one as well as another.' Then he adds, 'Strengthen your attack against the city and demolish it.'

cards.question: True or false: when Bathsheba hears that her husband is dead, she mourns for him.

cards.text: When the time of mourning is over, David has her brought to his house. She becomes his wife and bears him a son.

cards.question: From the outside, it all looks settled. But the passage ends with this: 'But the thing that David had done was ___ in the sight of the LORD.'

cards.text: I bet David thinks it's all buried. But the LORD saw it. And friend, this story is far from over.

findings.problem: The setup line says the next detail 'should stop any king in his tracks.' That rules out the two harmless wrong answers, 'a servant in the palace' and 'a visitor from Hebron,' and points straight to the right answer, that she is married.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: 'I think David's got a plan' gives a reason for David sending Uriah home. The text never says why David tells him to go home, so this adds a motive the text doesn't give, even with 'I think' in front of it. The Feelings rule allows guessing at a feeling. It doesn't allow adding a reason.

rule.text: Reasons. He never adds why someone did, said or thought something unless the text says why.

findings.problem: The joke compares Uriah's loyalty to a coupon that 'still believed in itself.' The coupon's trait is self-belief, not loyalty, so the comparison doesn't share Uriah's action of refusing comfort out of loyalty to the troops. A baker would have to work out why the coupon is the measure of loyalty.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: 'This is where the story turns dark' comes right before the question about what David's letter says. It rules out the two harmless wrong answers, 'Send him home to his wife for a while' and 'Make him a commander over the army,' and leaves only the right answer.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: Most story cards are flat retellings with no Papa Dorin voice, such as stop 1 cards 3, 8, 10, 12 and 17 and stop 2 cards 4, 6, 10, 12 and 14. Across 34 cards there are only two jokes and almost no laid-back or LOUD shifts. Jokes don't fit every moment in a passage about adultery and murder, but these cards don't have reactions, disbelief or storyteller lines either.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: Card 1 calls Joab 'his army commander.' That fact comes from outside the passage (for example 2 Samuel 8:16), but the card's verses field cites only 2 Samuel 11:1, and the card text gives no reference for it.
findings.question: How should a card cite an outside fact used to introduce someone? prep-walkthrough.md says such facts come 'with their reference,' but it also says a story card cites only the verses it tells, 'no wider and no narrower,' and the output has a single verses field. Should the outside reference go in the verses field, in the card text, or nowhere?

findings.problem: This passage centers on adultery and a planned killing. The docs say Papa Dorin is laugh-out-loud funny and that funny moments 'come up a lot,' but they also say his personality fits the moment. They give no guidance on how much humor, if any, belongs in passages about grave sin. Both jokes here (the loyal coupon and Joab's 'SCRIPT') sit right next to the murder plot.
findings.question: Should passages centered on serious sin, such as adultery or murder, have a lighter humor target or limits on where jokes can go, like not joking about the people carrying out the sin? Is a joke about Joab's thoroughness in covering up Uriah's death acceptable?
